sections.label: Reserve accumulation and its costs
sections.summary: Singapore's Reserve accumulation system involves costs from Singaporeans' sacrifices, including below-market land acquisitions and CPF balances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Singapore Government have put in place a good Reserve accumulation system, started by the late Dr Goh Keng Swee, to facilitate the accumulation of the huge Reserves we have today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: However, because our Reserves are not accumulated from natural resources, there is a cost to accumulating our Reserves, which comes from the sacrifices of the Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: For example, much of the land reserves came from the acquisitions of land from Singaporeans at below market prices during the 1970s and 1980s, while the financial reserves are accumulated through the investment of land sales proceeds, Government surpluses and the Central Provident Board (CPF) balances of Singaporeans.

sections.label: Estimating financial reserves
sections.summary: Hazel Poa will show financial reserves can be estimated at about $1.2 trillion by deducting liabilities from financial assets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: My colleague Ms Hazel Poa will show the House later that we can estimate our financial reserves to be about $1.2 trillion, simply by deducting the relevant liabilities from the financial assets.

sections.label: MAS accumulated new OFR
sections.summary: From end-2019 to end-2022, MAS accumulated about $250 billion in new OFR from large access foreign inflows.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: For example, from the end of 2019 to the end of 2022, even during the COVID-19 pandemic, MAS had accumulated new OFR from large access foreign inflows amounting to about $250 billion.

sections.label: Financial reserves generate NIR
sections.summary: The financial reserves currently generate NIR of about $50 billion a year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Currently, the financial reserves generate NIR of about $50 billion dollars a year.

sections.label: Financial reserves and investment returns
sections.summary: Singapore has about $1.2 trillion in financial reserves, growing yearly and generating $47 billion in fiscal 2023 investment returns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In summary, although not necessarily known and accepted by most Singaporeans, it is transparent to the financial markets that Singapore has approximately $1.2 trillion dollars of financial reserves, which is still growing every year and generating higher and higher investment returns each year amounting to $47 billion in fiscal year 2023.

sections.label: Budget surplus with NIRC
sections.summary: Total expenditures exceed operating revenues by $3 billion to $5 billion, so the budget should be in big surplus after NIRC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Total expenditures, which include both operating and development expenditures slightly exceeds the operating revenues by about $3 billion to $5 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, the budget should be in a big surplus after taking in the NIRC, which is $23.5 billion in fiscal year 2023.

sections.label: Capital transfer to endowment funds
sections.summary: Capital transfers to endowment and trust funds equalled 64% of NIRC from fiscal 2012 to 2020 and 72% in fiscal 2023, accumulating about $51 billion by end of fiscal 2023.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Based on the budget figures from fiscal year 2012 to 2020, the total capital transfer to the endowment and trust funds is equivalent to 64% of the total NIRC allocated to the budget in that period.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In fiscal year 2023, the transfer equalled 72% of the NIRC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As a result, about $51 billion has been accumulated in the 11 funds listed in the Government financial statements by the end of fiscal year 2023.

sections.label: Net spending of 11 funds
sections.summary: Between 2018 and 2022, actual net annual spending for the 11 funds was less than 10% of their total assets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Between 2018 and 2022, the actual net annual spending for the 11 funds, accounted for less than 10% of the total assets of the funds.

sections.label: HDB land cost payment
sections.summary: In fiscal year 2022, HDB paid about $5.39 billion of land cost to the financial reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In fiscal year 2022, the HDB paid about $5.39 billion of land cost to the financial reserves.

sections.label: HDB deficits in fiscal 2022
sections.summary: HDB is saddled with large deficits, which amounted to $5.38 billion in fiscal year 2022.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As a result, HDB is saddled with large deficits, which amounted to $5.38 billion in fiscal year 2022.

sections.label: PSP first proposal on funds
sections.summary: PSP's first proposal is that no further endowment and trust funds should be created and no further top-ups made to existing ones.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: PSP's first proposal is that no further endowment and trust funds should be created and no further top-ups should be made to existing endowment and trust funds.

sections.label: PSP second proposal on land cost
sections.summary: PSP's second proposal is to waive land cost for public housing owned by Singaporeans under its affordable home scheme, which may slow reserve accumulation by up to $5 billion a year and eliminate the HDB deficit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: PSP's second proposal is to waive the land cost for public housing owned by Singaporeans for the purpose of occupancy under the affordable home scheme, proposed by PSP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Assuming the very unlikely scenario, that all Singaporeans do not sell their HDB flat, waiving land cost for public housing, may slow down the accumulation of financial reserves by up to $5 billion a year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In addition, the affordable home scheme will eliminate the HDB deficit, releasing substantial resources back into the budget and reducing the tax burden of all Singaporeans, especially the middle-class Singaporeans.

sections.label: Reserves growth and fiscal space
sections.summary: PSP estimates reserves at $1.2 trillion with five growth sources, giving fiscal space to waive land cost for BTO pricing and delay tax rises.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: PSP has estimated that our financial reserves is about $1.2 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: I have also explained that there are five main sources of growth for our Reserves, which will enable it to continue growing, by tens of or even, sometimes, hundreds of billions of dollars a year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This provides us, with the fiscal space to relax the pace of our Reserve accumulation marginally by, perhaps, a few billion dollars a year to waive the land cost for BTO flat pricing and, deploy the surplus budget and NIRC resources more proactively, to delay and reduce the necessity to raise taxes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: While we agree that there are benefits in having Reserves to cope with unforeseen circumstances, we are of the view that there comes a point, beyond which, continued accumulation of Reserves hurts the welfare of and compromises the quality of life of present-day Singaporeans.

sections.label: Minimum reserves estimate
sections.summary: Adding Temasek assets and MAS OFR and RMGS gives a minimum financial reserves estimate of $1.09 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The value of the assets managed by GIC is secret.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But, even if we only add up, the assets under Temasek and the OFR and RMGS under MAS, we get a minimum estimate of the financial reserves of $1.09 trillion.

sections.label: Reserves size range estimate
sections.summary: Adding GFS net assets to MAS OFR and RMGS gives $1.36 trillion, so reserves are estimated between $1.09 trillion and $1.36 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: So, by adding up the net assets under GFS, and the OFR and RMGS under MAS, we arrive at a total of $1.36 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Hence, we believe that the size of the financial reserves is somewhere between $1.09 trillion and $1.36 trillion.

sections.label: GIC and CPF interest gap
sections.summary: The 1.4 percentage point gap between GIC returns and CPF interest paid goes into the Reserves, around $7 billion yearly.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The Minister for Manpower told us last year that CPF members earned, on average, an interest rate of close to 4%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This difference between the rate of return earned by GIC and that paid to CPF members of 1.4 percentage point goes directly into the Reserves and could now be around $7 billion per year.

sections.label: Reserve accumulation retirement cost
sections.summary: Reserve accumulation comes at the cost of lower retirement adequacy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Reserve accumulation, thus, comes at the cost of lower retirement adequacy.

sections.label: Reserves versus savings survey
sections.summary: Estimated accumulated Reserves of $1.2 trillion are 12 times annual expenditure, while a survey shows over half of Singaporean savings are under six months of salary.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: According to our estimates, the Government accumulated Reserves have reached $1.2 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This is 12 times the Government's annual expenditure.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: On the other hand, OCBC's 2023 National Financial Health Survey shows that over half of Singaporean savings are not even equivalent to six months of salary.

sections.label: New citizens and population
sections.summary: Without about 20,000 new citizens each year, the population will begin to shrink.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: If not for the annual intake of about 20,000 new citizens, our population will begin to shrink.

sections.label: Reserves and falling TFR
sections.summary: The Reserves are said to benefit children and grandchildren, but the TFR has fallen to 1.05, half the replacement rate of 2.1.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: We keep hearing that the Reserves are for the benefit of our children and grandchildren.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: But our TFR has fallen to 1.05, which is half the replacement rate of 2.1.

sections.label: Using more NIRC returns
sections.summary: The Government should not rule out using more than the current 50% of NIRC to lessen the taxation burden on Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: My second point is that the Government should not rule out using more than the current 50% of NIRC or what is known as the investment returns from the Reserves, to lessen the taxation burden on Singaporeans.

sections.label: Ong Teng Cheong's 50-50 formula
sections.summary: The 50% figure is not sacrosanct; in the 1990s up to 100% could be spent, and Ong Teng Cheong proposed a 50-50 formula.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The 50% figure is not a sacrosanct number.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the 1990s, the Government was free to spend up to 100% of the interest and dividends it earned on past Reserves within a current term of government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: When our first elected president, Ong Teng Cheong, was moved to speak on this, the late president's concern was whether the interest and dividends generated by past Reserves ought to be left fully in the hands of a current government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: He called on the PAP to stop using 100% of the net investment income (NII), and instead proposed a 50-50 formula, where 50% could be spent, and 50% of the investment returns would be added to the principal Reserves.

sections.label: IPS working paper release
sections.summary: In August last year, the Institute of Policy Studies released a working paper on Singapore's fiscal policies and National Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In August last year, the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) released a working paper titled Public Deliberation on Singapore's Fiscal Policies and National Reserves.

sections.label: IPS survey on NIR framework
sections.summary: The IPS working paper observed that survey respondents chose to maintain the 50-50 NIR framework, while budget game participants were more open to using more than 50%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The IPS working paper observed that while survey respondents chose to maintain the 50-50 NIR framework, the participants in the budget game were "more open to consider using more of the investment returns, that is, more than 50%, if these were spent in ways that would generate clear and measurable returns whether financial or social".

sections.label: WP NIRC utilisation increase
sections.summary: The WP has called for increasing use of the NIRC beyond 50% when needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What the WP has called for is an increase in the utilisation of the NIRC beyond 50% when needed.

sections.label: WP on Reserves use
sections.summary: The WP does not see using 60% of the NIRC as imprudent if there are justifiable reasons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If Mr Leong is right and the total value of our Reserves stands at $1.2 trillion dollars, COVID-19, the crisis of a generation, led to the consumption of about $40 billion, or 3.3% of our principal Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Extrapolating from Deputy Prime Minister's reply in this House, the $40 billion amount used for "the crisis of a generation" was recovered in two years or less through the sale of land and NIRC contributions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The WP certainly does not see the depth of our Reserves as a licence for the Government to spend beyond its means or to stop the growth of our principal Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But, the same way the PAP of the 1990s did not see it fiscally imprudent or irresponsible to use up to 100% of the investment returns on the principal Reserves if required, the WP does not see it as imprudent, for example, to use 60% of the NIRC, if there are justifiable reasons to do so.

sections.label: Ageing and investment returns
sections.summary: Inter-generational changes and a hyper-aged society should prompt consideration of using more investment returns for social needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To that and, thirdly, inter-generational changes and new realities, such as our transition to a hyper-aged society, should prompt us to consider whether more of our investment returns should be used to fund social needs, especially when we think of an older generation of Singaporeans who contributed relatively more in taxes and sacrificed for the greater good.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The words of the late Dr Richard Hu are not only true of the NII framework of the 1990s.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: That returning 50% of investment returns may not be appropriate in all circumstances going forward, particularly, in view of our rapidly ageing population.

sections.label: Standing Select Committee on Reserves
sections.summary: This House should set up a Standing Select Committee to look into the health of our Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: To take advantage of Parliament's sovereign status and its privileged role as an institution of public record, this House should set up a Standing Select Committee that looks into the health of our Reserves.

sections.label: Singapore OFR stock ranking
sections.summary: In 2019 Singapore had the 11th highest stock of OFRs, and third highest as a percentage of GDP and per capita.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In 2019, Singapore had the 11th highest stock of OFRs in the world.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: As a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP) and on a per capita basis, it was the third highest in the world.

sections.label: Constitutional amendments on Reserves
sections.summary: Two Constitution amendments related to Reserves occurred: in 2009 instituting the NIR framework and in 2015 including Temasek.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: During my tenure as a Member of Parliament so far, we have had two amendments to the Constitution related to our Reserves: first, in 2009, to institute the NIR framework; and, in 2015, when we included Temasek in the NIR framework.

sections.label: Foreign exchange market growth
sections.summary: The foreign exchange market has ballooned more than five times since 1997, with average daily trading volume of about $7 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Today, the foreign exchange market has since ballooned more than five times since 1997, with an average trading volume of about $7 trillion a day.

sections.label: Global Financial Crisis deposit guarantee
sections.summary: During the Global Financial Crisis, the Government provided a $150 billion guarantee on all bank deposits in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: During the Global Financial Crisis, the Government provided a $150 billion guarantee on all bank deposits in Singapore.

sections.label: Strong Reserves crisis response
sections.summary: Strong Reserves gave the Government fiscal ability during COVID-19 to boost healthcare, obtain vaccines early and introduce support packages like the Job Support Scheme.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The second critical advantage of strong Reserves is our ability to mount a strong response during a crisis.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: We have seen that playing a crucial role during the COVID-19 pandemic, giving the Government the fiscal ability to significantly boost healthcare measures, procure and obtain the best vaccines amongst the earliest in the world and introduce huge support packages, such as the Job Support Scheme (JSS).

sections.label: Growing NIRC contribution
sections.summary: The stable and growing NIRC is expected to contribute $23.48 billion in FY2023, about one-fifth of annual revenue, up from $7.6 billion in 2012 and $16.41 billion in 2018.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Fourthly, the stable and growing NIRC, is another critical advantage that we have.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Thanks to decades of prudence and accumulation by those before us, our Reserves now generate a significant stable and sustainable income stream to fund annual Budgets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Based on financial year (FY) 2023 estimates, the NIRC is expected to contribute $23.48 billion, or about one-fifth of our annual revenue; second to corporate tax.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Ten years ago, in 2012, the NIRC was $7.6 billion, about one-third of what it is today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Five years ago, in 2018, it was $16.41 billion.

sections.label: Cost-of-living support package
sections.summary: In September 2023 the Government announced a $1.1 billion Cost-of-Living support package, and the speaker calls for similar help in a fiscally responsible way.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: For example, in September 2023, the Government announced the $1.1 billion Cost-of-Living support package to provide relief to households.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: I also remember during the pandemic, we had additional budgets, a total of five Budgets in one-over year, to help Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Here, I call on the Government to do that to help present-day Singaporeans cope with the cost of living, including in the coming Budget, and doing it in a fiscally responsible and sustainable way.

sections.label: Proposed amendments to motion
sections.summary: The amendments delete "review" and insert "ensure", insert "always stay fiscally responsible and sustainable", and delete "continuing to save" and insert "planning and providing".

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: First, in line 1, to delete "review" and insert "ensure".

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: Third, in line 2, after the words "Reserve accumulation policies", to insert "always stay fiscally responsible and sustainable,".

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: And fourth, in line 3, to delete "continuing to save" and insert "planning and providing".

sections.label: Reserves size disclosure limits
sections.summary: Mr Leong Mun Wai asks whether the size of the Reserves can be disclosed; the speaker says this is unwise because others would know the limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: The point that Mr Leong Mun Wai is trying to say is, can we still let everyone know the size of our Reserves?

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: I do not think it is a wise thing because once people know where our limit is, then, next time around, when they know where they can push.

sections.label: MAS OFR amount
sections.summary: The current amount of Official Foreign Reserves that MAS has is already 100% of Singapore's GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The current amount of OFR that MAS has is already 100% of our GDP.

sections.label: Keeping last trump card secret
sections.summary: The speaker says the last trump card should be kept secret, and that Singapore's financial reserves are its only back-stop as a tiny island-state.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: If there is a speculative attack, we never know what the reason is.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: It could be some events that happened that caused the speculative attack.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: Therefore, we always want to keep that last trump card to ourselves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: I believe that usually works because if we reveal too much, that is when we show our hand, where our limits are.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: But, more importantly, the point about Singapore is that we have our inherent vulnerabilities, unlike other countries where they have a big domestic economy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: For Singapore, we are just a tiny island-state and the financial reserves is just the only back-stop that we have.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
sentences.text: Therefore, we need to really be mindful that someone may see us as a tiny state and may, one day, find a reason to attack us.

sections.label: Official definition of Reserves
sections.summary: In Singapore, Reserves are officially defined as the net assets of Fifth Schedule entities in the Constitution, including GIC, Temasek, CPF, HDB, JTC and MAS.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In Singapore, Reserves are officially defined as the net assets of the Fifth Schedule entities in the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This includes holdings by not just our sovereign wealth funds (SWFs), GIC and Temasek, but also CPF, HDB, JTC and MAS.

sections.label: Reserves belong to people
sections.summary: The nation's Reserves belong to the people, not the Government, and the Government is the steward of the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Our nation's Reserves belong therefore to the people, not to the Government.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It means that our Government is the steward of our Reserves.

sections.label: Transparency and concealed GIC assets
sections.summary: Transparency ensures reserves are accountable in real time to their owners, so the concealed assets of GIC run afoul of this principle.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Generally, such transparency also ensures that reserves are held accountable in real time to their owners.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: This is why the current practice where the portfolio assets of Temasek and the foreign exchange holdings of MAS are known, but the assets of GIC remain concealed, runs afoul of this principle.

sections.label: Reserves size versus GDP
sections.summary: MAS judges business-as-usual exchange rate management needs 65% to 75% of GDP, while reserves from MAS, Temasek and GIC exceed $1.2 trillion, close to twice GDP.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In any case, MAS has, itself, adjudged that the amount required for business-as-usual management of our exchange rate regime amounts to between 65% and 75% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Official data reveals that reserves from MAS and Temasek, together with the publicly acknowledged amount of at least $100 billion from GIC, means that it is in excess of $1.2 trillion, as PSP has suggested.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Even with this lower bound, which is likely to understate the size of our Reserves, is already close to twice our GDP, multiples more that of what the Government has itself stated is reasonable for defending our currency.

sections.label: Japan pension fund openness
sections.summary: The Government Pension Fund of Japan, the world's largest single SWF, is open about its assets and performance.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The world's largest single SWF, the Government Pension Fund of Japan, is open about its assets and performance.

sections.label: SWF Russian assets scrutiny
sections.summary: The public cannot scrutinise whether SWFs inadvertently hold Russian assets tied to sanctioned individuals or entities, though some information is reported to MAS.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For example, while some information is presumably reported to MAS as the regulator, the public does not know and is unable to scrutinise if SWFs may inadvertently hold Russian assets tied to sanctioned individual or entities.

sections.label: GIC and Temasek investment focus
sections.summary: The speaker suggests GIC focus on global investments for diversification while Temasek focuses more on local opportunities.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: With such a long horizon, it would be better to be more aggressive in investing, in putting our money to work by, perhaps, investing more domestically than we do today.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: That is why I believe that it makes sense for GIC to train its eyes toward global investments for international diversification benefits, while Temasek focuses much more on local opportunities, supporting the efforts of Singaporeans to reinvest in their home country.

sections.label: Reserve interest and NIRC formula
sections.summary: Any income not set aside as saving reduces the Reserves, so the argument applies equally to the 2008 NIRC formula change and Temasek's 2015 addition.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: After all, any amount of income that we choose not to set aside as saving, even one cent, would logically amount to taking away from the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: So, if it is applied to WP's suggestion, that we could avoid a hike in the GST by reducing the share of reserve interest, not the principal, but interest, that is being returned to Reserves, it should apply with equal force when the PAP chose to alter the formula for NII to introduce the NIRC in 2008 or to add Temasek to the framework in 2015.

sections.label: Santiago principles transparency accountability
sections.summary: Transparency, accountability and consultation are foundational Santiago principles signed by GIC and Temasek, but GIC fares poorly on transparency and Temasek is opaque on governance accountability.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It amounts to suggesting to parents, who want to create a better environment for their kids by having to spend more of their tuition fees or creating a better home environment, that they do not really know any better.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It would not surprise Members of this House that the three principles I outlined of transparency, accountability and consultation are foundational ones, embedded in the Santiago principles – a set of best practices that sovereign investments agreed to by the International Working Group of Sovereign Wealth Funds, for which, GIC and Temasek, are signatories.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: GIC, however, fares poorly on a range of transparency indicators and Temasek is particularly opaque on its accountability surrounding governance structures.

sections.label: Pandemic Reserves drawdown
sections.summary: The Government drew down Reserves during COVID-19 for public health, vaccines, support packages and a $150 million deposit guarantee.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Government drew down Reserves for public health expenditure, including securing of vaccines and the roll-out of stabilisation and support packages, to help workers stay employed and provide support for businesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Such policies helped us emerge stronger when the economy recovered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Also, setting aside $150 million of Reserves to guarantee deposits was one of the measures that were instrumental in safeguarding the continuity of business operations.

sections.label: Global Financial Crisis Jobs Credit
sections.summary: Reserves drawdown during the 2008 and 2009 Global Financial Crisis helped maintain jobs, including through the Jobs Credit scheme.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Let us also not forget how the draw down on the Reserves helped maintain jobs in Singapore during the Global Financial Crisis in 2008 and 2009.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: One very successful scheme was the Jobs Credit scheme which helped business leaders maintain a higher employment level than what would have been possible otherwise.

sections.label: Reserves trade-offs and confidentiality
sections.summary: The passage states there are trade-offs and that the exact size and details of Singapore's Reserves should be confidential.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: There are no free lunches in life, and we should be very, very clear of what the trade-offs that are involved here.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Also, in my view, the exact size and details of Singapore's Reserves should be confidential to reduce the chance of speculative attacks by any foreign institution.

sections.label: NIRC 50% spending limit
sections.summary: The speaker disagrees with not limiting NIRC use to 50%, saying the limit preserves principal and ensures prudent fiscal management.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Responding to the suggestion that the Singapore Government should not limit the use of up to 50% of the NIRC, I respectfully disagree.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: By spending only a portion of the investment returns, the Government aims to and will be able to preserve the principal value of the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Additionally, limiting the use of the NIRC to only 50% ensures prudent fiscal management both in terms of taxation as well as government expenditure.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Realised returns can be lower or higher, so the 50% rule also protects the principal in those scenarios.

sections.label: Reserves as economic buffer
sections.summary: The Reserves act as a critical buffer against economic volatility and provide financial security, as seen during the pandemic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Our Reserves act as a critical buffer against economic volatility and provide financial security, as seen recently during the pandemic.

sections.label: Fifth safeguard NIR framework
sections.summary: The passage quotes the then-Finance Minister on a fifth safeguard in the NIR framework's governance processes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The fifth safeguard and I will read what the then-Finance Minister said, and I quote, "but there is an important fifth safeguard, which is in the governance processes in the NIR framework that also ensures that we do not spend on the basis of over-optimistic assumptions about the expected returns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The process by which expected long-term real rate of returns are decided has checks and balances and is shaped by a sense of realism about the risks in the investment world." In response to that, I would be grateful if the hon Member could agree with me that the way the NIRC system is designed, actually ameliorates the concern that the Member has about the expected future rates of return.

sections.label: Reserves disclosure and inflation
sections.summary: He asks whether this is an added reason for not disclosing the Reserves, since more money in the money supply causes inflation if the asset pool is unchanged.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Is he putting this up as an additional reason for not disclosing the Reserves?

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
sentences.text: I did, because the more money you put into the overall money supply, whether the Government spends it or any private entity spends it, it will lead to inflation if the overall pool of assets does not change.

sections.label: Reserves discovery and populist policies
sections.summary: He says discovering the Reserves' size could push the Government into populist policies causing inflation, and notes two points preserved in the amended Motion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
sentences.text: What I had said, just to be very clear, is, if there is a discovery of the size of the overall Reserves which pushes the Government into extra populist policies, that will cause inflation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
sentences.text: Meaning, the populist policies that are mandated will lead to inflation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant
sentences.text: I do not think that is something that the Government can answer.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: There are two main points the original Motion made that are preserved in the amended Motion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: These are: the Budget should help reduce the financial burdens of Singaporeans and improve their quality of life; the second is the Reserve accumulation policy should be adequate for future generations of Singaporeans.

sections.label: NII funding and preserving Reserves
sections.summary: Part of the NII from the Reserves funds the annual Budget, now its largest component, so the Reserves must be preserved and prudently invested.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Part of the NII from these Reserves now fund our annual Budget every year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The amount this is provided has grown significantly over the years, such that it is now the largest component of our annual Budget.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: For this benefit to continue for future generations, we must ensure that the Reserves are preserved, prudently invested and that some of the returns also go back to the Reserve to take into account the effects of inflation and if possible, allow for modest real growth as well; meaning, growth adjusted for inflation.

sections.label: Life expectancy since 1959
sections.summary: Since the PAP came to power in 1959, life expectancy has grown from 63.87 years to 84.39 years, one of the world's longest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Since 1959, when the PAP first came to power, our life expectancy has grown from 63.87 years to 84.39 years now, one of the longest in the world.

sections.label: Vouchers for lowest-income Singaporeans
sections.summary: Singapore is one of few governments distributing vouchers based on Government Budgets, and for lowest-income Singaporeans these exceed the rise in cost of living.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Again, we are one of the few governments that has a wide-ranging scheme of distributing vouchers to Singaporeans based on our Government Budgets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: For the lowest-income Singaporeans, these vouchers would be significantly more than the increase in cost of living.

sections.label: Which Reserves are known
sections.summary: Much of the Reserves is in the open, such as MAS' and Temasek's assets, while only GIC, the third pot, is unknown.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: A good part of the Reserves are in the open, such as MAS' assets as well as Temasek's assets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: It is only the third port, GIC, which is unknown.

sections.label: Land sales and Reserves
sections.summary: Land sold on 99-year leases is treated as an asset because the cash goes into the Reserves, and launching HDB flats without land costs could crash the market.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Land is an asset even if sold at 99-year leases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Since it is a translation of a physical asset into a cash asset, that cash goes into the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: And the income from that Reserves will be part of the NIR.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: We are selling one asset and translating into another; therefore, it is still treated as an asset.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I think the two additional arguments that we went through in some detail about the effect of the PSP's housing policy was that, first of all, if you launch new HDB flats at prices that do not include land, they are likely to cause a crash on the existing market, because many other people have much higher HDB values which are significant assets for them.

sections.label: Trust in PAP Government
sections.summary: A study ranked the PAP Government highest for trust on the Reserves, with an average score of 7.26 out of 10.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: I have managed to have a look at the study and one of the points he did not make in the study was that the entity that ranked the highest – and this was actually very humbling for me when I read it because there is quite a lot of cynicism out there – but the entity that was ranked the highest in the study for trust for input on the Reserves was the PAP Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This is on a scale of one to 10 – it was given a score of 7.26 on average by participants.

sections.label: Opposition check on spending
sections.summary: The Opposition and backbench should check Government spending, and any Opposition policy requiring more spending must explain its cost.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: The Government and successive Governments have essentially built a nation with prudent spending.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: They have saved enough and the Government itself, which is the custodian of spending, is not saying it needs more money.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: So, to me, the real job of the Opposition and the backbench is really to be a check on Government spending because there is usually a perverse incentive for government to spend too much.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: So, if a government is saying that it can meet its current objectives with the current budget, there is no need to spend more.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: If the political Opposition is coming forward with different policies that require more spending, then it is for them to bear that onus to explain what the cost the policy is – not the Government.

sections.label: Sale proceeds into Reserves
sections.summary: Proceeds from selling land or Government-held shares must go back into the asset pool of the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: Companies may not last 99 years, but if you sell shares in a company, that is also treated as an asset.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
sentences.text: So, the sale of land, the sale of shares that the Government may hold, all of these must go back into the asset pool of the Reserves.

sections.label: MAS optimal OFR range
sections.summary: MAS assessed the optimal Official Foreign Reserves amount as between 65% and 75% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: MAS has assessed that the "optimal" amount of OFR it needs to provide a "strong buffer" against stresses in the global economy and market is between 65% and 75% of GDP.

sections.label: MAS OFR above optimal
sections.summary: As at September 2023, MAS' OFR was $455.5 billion or 70% of GDP, with potential to reach 106% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Based on a Parliamentary reply by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong to me, as at September 2023, MAS' current OFR stood at $455.5 billion or 70% of GDP, with the potential to ramp it up to 106% of GDP by redeeming the RMGS holdings of $237.6 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This means MAS effectively has access to 31% more foreign reserves than the high-end of the range it assesses to be optimal to defend the Singapore dollar.

sections.label: Extreme tail-risk scenarios warning
sections.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Wong said Singapore must brace for extreme tail-risk scenarios, including crises causing capital outflows beyond MAS' Reserves or emergencies threatening the economy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In a Parliamentary reply on 3 October 2023, Deputy Prime Minister Wong said that we need to brace for extreme tail-risk scenarios, including crises of unprecedented scale that could lead to significant capital outflows beyond MAS' Reserves, or emergencies caused by state or non-state actors threatening our economy, livelihoods or national existence.

sections.label: Confidential sharing of Reserves figures
sections.summary: Reserves figures could be shared confidentially with MPs or the cross-party standing finance Select Committee if the Government wants strategic ambiguity on the full size.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If the Government wishes to maintain a strategic ambiguity regarding the full size of the Reserves, the figures could be shared confidentially with MPs or with the cross-party standing finance Select Committee that looks into the health of our Reserves and Government finances, which the Leader of the Opposition has proposed.

sections.label: Jobs Support Scheme spending impact
sections.summary: About $28 billion was spent on JSS, and an estimated 165,000 local jobs were preserved.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The impact: the amount that was spent on JSS was about $28 billion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: And a total – just to remind everyone – of an estimated 165,000 local jobs were preserved.

sections.label: President's approval for Past Reserves
sections.summary: The Government can only draw on the Past Reserves with the approval of the President.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The Government can only draw on the Past Reserves with the approval of the President.

sections.label: NIRC contribution to Budget
sections.summary: NIRC contributed 20% to the annual Budget for FY2022 and is estimated to be the second largest for FY2023.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: NIRC is a large contributor to the annual Budget at 20% for FY2022 and estimated to be the second largest for FY2023.

sections.label: Adult Singaporeans benefiting from Package
sections.summary: An estimated 2.9 million adult Singaporeans will benefit from this Package.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: An estimated 2.9 million adult Singaporeans will benefit from this Package.

sections.label: CDC voucher disbursement January
sections.summary: The most recent disbursement was in January this year, when every Singaporean household received $500 in CDC vouchers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The most recent disbursement was in January this year where every Singaporean household received $500 in CDC vouchers.

sections.label: Means-tested support and eligibility
sections.summary: Progressive, means-tested tax and support measures mean many households do not meet eligibility criteria or receive full benefits, and more may be needed for this group.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: Because our system of tax is progressive and it is means-tested for most of the support measures, many of the households do not meet the eligibility criteria and they do not receive the full benefits of some of the support packages.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: But I do want to say that given the current prolonged nature of the uncertainties and the slower growth, we may have to look at doing more for this group of people.

sections.label: Taxes, Reserves and NIR framework
sections.summary: Funding comes from taxes and Reserves, and adhering to not overspending revenue and protecting Past Reserves enables balance; under the NIR framework the Government can spend up to 50% of long-term expected real returns.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: The reality is that funding comes from taxes, from how we spend our Past Reserves and how we accumulate our Reserves, and hence adhering to the principles of not spending more than the revenue within that term of government and protecting our Past Reserves has and will enable us to achieve this balance.

sentences.speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
sentences.text: So, I would say that I cannot support the original Motion, and I support the amended Motion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Under the NIR framework, the Government can spend up to 50% of the long-term expected real returns on relevant assets.

sections.label: Reserves belong to the people
sections.summary: The nation's Reserves belong to the people, not the Government of the day, and stewards must be accountable to all Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: As my Parliamentary colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim shared, our nation's Reserves belong to the people, not the Government of the day.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is important for the stewards of the Reserves to be accountable to not just the Government but to all Singaporeans, the key stakeholders of our Reserves.

sections.label: GIC returns to CPF members
sections.summary: The passage asks whether GIC's returns can be passed through to CPF members.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Can we not allow GIC's returns to be passed through to CPF members?

sections.label: GIC returns versus CPF OA rate
sections.summary: Using 20-year nominal GIC returns of 6.9% and the CPF OA rate of 2.5%, CPF monies double in about 10 years versus 29 years, greatly affecting retirement savings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Based on the 20-year nominal returns of the GIC portfolio of 6.9% and the CPF OA rate of 2.5%, just based on a simple rule of 72, the number of years it takes for our CPF monies to double goes from about 10 years based on GIC's returns, to 29 years based on the prevailing CPF OA rate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The effects on our ability to save for our own retirement is clearly tremendous.

sections.label: CPF Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme
sections.summary: The speaker has urged the Government to implement the CPF Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme, noting GIC's 20-year returns exceed the 2.5% OA interest rate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In each of the last three years, I have been urging the Government to implement the CPF Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme (LRIS) to better support Singaporeans' retirement needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: And based on public records, GIC's 20-year returns have been consistently above the 2.5% interest rate offered to OA.

sections.label: Using more than 50% NIRC
sections.summary: The Government should not rule out using more than the current 50% of the NIRC to alleviate the burden on Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The second point is: the Government should not rule out using more than the current 50% of the NIRC to alleviate the burden on Singaporeans.

sections.label: WP proposal on NIRC use
sections.summary: The WP proposes using more of the NIRC to alleviate people's burden, denying it raids Reserves or eats next year's grain, and supports Mr Leong Mun Wai's Motion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The WP proposes to use more of the NIRC to alleviate people's burden.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The intention is not to raid the Reserves, nor is it "寅吃卯粮" (In English): Eating next year's grain this year, as misinterpreted by the Deputy Prime Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: We simply hope to achieve a better balance: the Reserves will continue to grow, but at a slower pace, so that we can take care of the livelihood of this generation of Singaporeans, provide timely assistance to the people, and continue to save for future generations. : I support the original Motion as filed by Mr Leong Mun Wai.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: We have been in the Chamber for over six-and-a-half hours, so, I propose to take a break now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.30 pm.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 5.07 pm until 5.30 pm.

sections.label: Government spending and NIRC
sections.summary: Government spending is around 18% of GDP and expected to rise, while NIRC has averaged around 3.5% of GDP, so Budget 2022 tax changes were needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Government spending stands now at around 18% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: MOF in its Occasional Paper states it expects to it increase to around 19% to 20% of GDP in the FY2026 to 2030 period and possibly exceed 20% of GDP by FY2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: This is due to our ageing population, rising utilisation of healthcare and medical inflation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: I just want to highlight that we also enjoy additional non-tax revenues through the NIRC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: The NIRC has averaged around 3.5% of GDP and we expect it to remain at about the same share of GDP over the coming years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: This would not have been sufficient to cover the increase in Government spending expected over the coming years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: That is why the tax changes announced in Budget 2022, including the GST increase, were necessary to close the funding gap.

sections.label: Singapore dollar forex turnover
sections.summary: BIS 2022 data shows Singapore dollar forex turnover at about US$182 billion daily, and rapid forex moves could wipe out over $1 trillion of Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: On the Singapore dollar front, I highlight latest data from BIS Triennial 2022 which shows that Singapore dollar foreign exchange (forex) turnover is about US$182 billion, in terms of daily average turnover, 2% of total market value.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: And this is about $6.6 trillion from the BIS survey in terms of global forex turnover.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Some Members had highlighted the rough estimates of about $1.2 trillion value in Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: That actual amount is quite minute – if the forex markets move in within six to seven days against the Singapore dollar, it could wipe out slightly more than $1 trillion in terms of dollar amounts, very rapidly.

sections.label: Low income tax and currency stability
sections.summary: Singapore's personal income tax is among the world's lowest and progressive, and currency stability comes from good Reserves and Budget policy.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Hence, Singapore's personal income tax rate is among the lowest in the world.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: It is also a relatively progressive system where only about 40% of the workforce pays any income tax at all.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: In addition, the Singapore currency is also stable and provides Singaporeans with a strong purchasing power.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: So, as several Members had mentioned earlier, the stability of the Singapore currency does not happen on its own; it happens because of our good policy on Reserves and our Budget policy that is solid, sound and based on strong principles, thus providing opportunities for Singaporean workers, our people, to get good jobs, and also to support past and future budgets. : Mr Deputy Speaker, one thing that I think this whole House can agree on is that the ongoing cost of living pressures, which form a key issue, is something that we must continue to manage today.

sections.label: NIRC funds annual Budget
sections.summary: NIRC provides 50% of net investment returns to fund about 20% of the annual Budget, including the Assurance Package.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Through the NIRC, 50% of the net investment returns or income on our reserves are used to fund about 20% of our annual Budget.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: This then goes into things like the Assurance Package, which saw most households receive $500 CDC vouchers and more to spend on food, groceries and other necessities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Without the NIRC, that means that the Government would need to collect 25% more of revenue, most likely through increased taxes.

sections.label: NIRC split for generations
sections.summary: The Government set the NIRC at 50%, half for the present generation and half for the future generation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: So, as any parent would tell you, the best we can do is to make sure that they are put in the best position to confront and conquer those challenges.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Hence, the Government has set the NIRC at 50%, half for the present generation and half for the future generation.

sections.label: 2008 Reserves for jobs
sections.summary: During the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, $4.9 billion of Reserves was used to support schemes helping workers and companies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Similarly, in the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, we could dip into $4.9 billion of our Reserves to support schemes to help workers retain jobs and offer liquidity to companies as well as for risk-sharing purposes.

sections.label: Hong Kong budget deficit
sections.summary: For April 2023 to March 2024, Hong Kong predicted a HK$54.4 billion deficit but accumulated HK$164 billion in eight months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: For the period April 2023 to March 2024, they announced in February 2023 a predicted Budget deficit of HK$54.4 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: However, it was announced recently that in the first eight months of their financial year, the government had accumulated a deficit of HK$164 billion, three times the predicted deficit and there are another four more months to go.

sections.label: Old age support ratio defined
sections.summary: In Singapore, the old age support ratio is the number of people aged 20 to 64 to those aged 65 and older.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: In Singapore, the old age support ratio is defined as the number of people aged 20 to 64 to the number of people aged 65 and older.

sections.label: Old age support ratio 2023
sections.summary: In 2023, the old age support ratio dropped to 3.7.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: In 2023, the ratio has dropped to 3.7.

sections.label: NIRC use limit
sections.summary: Only up to 50% of the NIRC can be used by the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Only up to 50% of the NIRC can be used by the Government.

sections.label: NIRC share of revenue
sections.summary: NIRC is 20% of total Government revenue, which the speaker feels is not low.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: But I may be opening a pandora's box as I make my next comment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: So, what it means that if I take NIRC as a percentage of total Government revenue, it is 20%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: From a risk management point of view, having 20% coming from what I ‒ my personal view ‒ feel is a passive sort of income, is not low.

sections.label: Corporate income tax revenue
sections.summary: Corporate income tax revenue for nine months is about $23.9 billion, so it will outstrip NIRC this year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Which is also why I was very happy when I read last week in the newspapers that our corporate income tax revenue for the first nine months is about $23.9 billion, comparable to what we have budgeted for the entire year for corporate income tax revenue.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Which means to say that for this year we can be certain that corporate income tax revenue will outstrip NIRC and that is a good thing.

sections.label: Small country bottom line
sections.summary: As a small country, Singapore does not want others to know its bottom line.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Because we are a small country, we do not want anyone to know where our bottom line is, because if others know your bottom line, they will know how to attack you.

sections.label: Cost of living and Motion
sections.summary: The Government introduced programs for the rising cost of living, and the speaker supports the amendments to the Motion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Just now, some Opposition Members mentioned the rise in the cost of living.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: Because of this, the Government has introduced a series of programs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
sentences.text: I do not know if everyone has heard of an old saying, "Every difficulty can be overcome." In our journey, in a country's journey, there are certainly many difficult stages, but as long as fellow Singaporeans unite, work hard and have a common goal, we will definitely overcome every difficulty.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: However, I support the amendments to the Motion as proposed by Mr Liang Eng Hwa, and let me explain why.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: On the face of it, the PSP’s Motion seems unobjectionable.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: After all, what is wrong with calling on the Government to review its current Budget and Reserve accumulation policies in order to help present-day Singaporeans with their financial burdens and improve their quality of life?

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
sentences.text: However, when you look at it carefully, the Motion implies various things which I cannot agree with.

sections.label: CPF interest rates
sections.summary: The Government has provided minimum CPF interest rates and does not cut them even when GIC's returns fall below.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Over the past 20 years of low interest rates, the Government has continued to provide members with 2.5% minimum interest on OA monies, and since 2008, a 4% minimum interest on Special, MediSave and Retirement Account (SMRA) monies, extra 1% interest on the first $60,000 of combined CPF balances for all members and an additional 1% interest on the first $30,000 of combined CPF balances for members aged 55 and above.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: While the Government expects to earn returns over the long term that will be able to cover CPF interest rates, there is no assurance that GIC's returns will exceed CPF interest rates in the shorter term, let alone every year.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: There have been years where GIC's returns fall below CPF interest rates, but we do not cut CPF interest rates.

sections.label: NIRC stable at 3.5% GDP
sections.summary: NIRC has stayed stable at about 3.5% of GDP over five years and this trend is expected to continue.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Over the past five years, NIRC has remained stable at about 3.5% of GDP and we expect this trend to continue.

sections.label: WP position on GST
sections.summary: The WP acknowledged a medium-term funding gap and need for tax raises, opposed past GST increases, and now accepts GST at 7%.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The WP has acknowledged that there is a medium-term funding gap and that taxes need to be raised.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: They opposed all the previous GST increases, but recently changed their position and said they accept the GST at 7%.

sections.label: GST increase with vouchers
sections.summary: The GST increase was done together with enhancements to the permanent GST vouchers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Remember, the GST increase was done together with enhancements to the permanent GST vouchers.

sections.label: Spending 50% of investment returns
sections.summary: 50% of investment returns is spent while the remaining 50% goes back into the Reserves to grow it for the future.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Today, we preserve our principal and strike a balance between our current and future needs by spending 50% of the investment returns, while putting the remaining 50% back into the Reserves to grow it for the future.

sections.label: Reserves as crisis ballast
sections.summary: Reserves provide ballast, having seen four major crises between 1997 and 2020, and can be drawn on in a crisis.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Not for now because we need to make sure that we have enough ballast to keep us going.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: We have faced four major crises between 1997 and 2020 – the Asian Financial Crisis, the SARS outbreak, Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In a crisis, we can draw on our Reserves, but having such solid Reserves in itself also means that we have a rock on which to anchor ourselves in turbulent times.

sections.label: Stewards managing the Reserves
sections.summary: As stewards of the Reserves, there is an obligation to manage it judiciously and make refinements where needed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: As stewards of our Reserves, we have the obligation to manage it judiciously, make refinements where needed, so that it will continue to serve its purpose for Singaporeans today and in years to come.

sections.label: Parliament committee annual review proposal
sections.summary: The report says Parliament could set up an ongoing committee convening an annual review, and that engagement must be carefully calibrated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: So, I suppose the argument can work both ways.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I refer to page 64 of the report which states quite clearly that, "another alternative is for the Parliament of Singapore to set up an ongoing committee that convenes an annual review", and it goes on.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: With regard to the proposal for a Select Committee and better engagement, it says, "This process needs to be carefully calibrated so that knowledgeable and activist segments of the population do not feel that it is an attempt to breed the siege mentality or reinforce what has been termed as the veil of vulnerability.

sections.label: Land resale and NIRC interest
sections.summary: The state can resell land depending on land use rules, and knowledge of this fact explains interest in more equitable NIRC use.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And the state, depending on what the prevailing land use rules are, can resell that piece of land.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And this is the point that I sought to put into my speech, which brings the ultimate conclusion, that para – and I will repeat it – it is the knowledge of this intuitive fact that the same piece of land can be resold and the state receives land sale receipts, why there is significant interest in conversations about a more equitable use of the NIRC for current and future generations of Singaporeans.

sections.label: Losing land use for 99 years
sections.summary: The speaker says Minister Tan See Leng's point was more a comment than a clarification and does not detract from losing land use for 99 years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: That was the essential point I was making.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I understand the point, which in Minister Tan See Leng's words, is more of a comment than a clarification, but it does not really detract from what I said, which is that we lose the use of the land for the 99 years, when we could have used it for other purposes.

sections.label: Investing and streaming out NIRC
sections.summary: The passage states that the funds are taken, invested and used sustainably by streaming them out through the NIRC.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: What we do is we take it, we invest it and we use it, but we use it in a sustainable manner by streaming it out through the NIRC.

sections.label: Confirming prompt public use of land
sections.summary: The question asks the Minister to confirm that all land acquired under the Land Acquisition Act since the 1970s was promptly used for public purposes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Can the Minister confirm that all the land acquired by the Government in the process of all these Land Acquisition Act acquisitions since the 1970s till now, that all the land has been promptly used for public purposes, within a certain number of years after acquisition?

sections.label: Government land acquisition purposes
sections.summary: The Minister says much acquired land would have been used for public purposes, with some kept in Reserves for strategic reasons.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: On the question of land acquisition, well, I do not have details with me, but I can say that much of the land would have been used for public purposes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Some of it may have to go into our land Reserves, but for strategic reasons, we may not want to use the land immediately, but we would have long-term plans for it or we may need to keep that land as a buffer zone.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, the short answer is, when the Government acquires land, it does so for a public purpose or a national purpose.

sections.label: Land value and auction
sections.summary: The passage states roads now go through the land, its value increased, the grandfather was paid $60,000 in the early 1980s, and the land was auctioned today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: So, now, we have got roads going through the land, and the land, to be fair, has increased in value.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: But the grandfather was paid $60,000 in the early 1980s and only today, the land was auctioned.

sections.label: Land Acquisition Act acquisition
sections.summary: The passage states the land was acquired under the Land Acquisition Act at that time and will be deployed when required.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: At that time when the land was acquired, it was acquired based on the Land Acquisition Act at that time; and when it is required to be deployed, it will be deployed.

sections.label: CPF members and GIC expertise
sections.summary: The passage asks what stops allowing CPF members to access GIC fund management expertise, noting 23% have investment accounts and 11% active accounts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: So, already we are allowing CPF members to invest their CPF investment accounts, but what is actually stopping us from allowing members to be able to access the fund management expertise of GIC to allow them to earn higher rates of return over the longer term in a selective manner?

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: This is where the latest statistics that I saw suggest – that only about 23% of CPF members have an investment account, but only 11% of CPF members have active accounts.

sections.label: Asset conversion not revenue
sections.summary: The passage states removing the temptation to push prices higher and that it is not revenue but converting an asset from one form to another.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: We remove the temptation to push the price higher because that becomes the only source of revenue or major source of revenue.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But before we even get there, we must go back to the fundamental point – which is that it is not revenue.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: We are just converting the asset from one form to another.

sections.label: Endowment and trust fund transfers
sections.summary: The passage states a pool of money is available for spending, and out of $124 billion in fiscal year 2023 about $17 billion moved to endowment and trust funds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: This becomes a pool of money that is available for spending.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: But the Minister will not dispute the fact that out of this $124 billion, in fiscal year 2023, about $17 billion is moved to the endowment funds and the trust fund.

sections.label: NIRC revenue and funds
sections.summary: The passage states capital is locked away, 20% of revenue comes from NIRC, revenue is fungible, and funds like Pioneer Generation, Merdeka Generation and GST Voucher are drawn down now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: So, on these two points, the capital is locked away and some of the capital is actually not for welfare spending, even for all these very long-term infrastructure spending – which should be dealt with in a different way, like what the Minister has said, there is a SINGA Fund, there are other things that we can use to finance all this.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: It is actually a very straightforward principle: 20% of our revenue comes from NIRC.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, the entire revenue is fungible, as Mr Leong said.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I did not say – and I am not sure why Mr Leong thinks so – that we take just that 20% slice of NIRC and park that in a fund.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: It all comes into the big pool of revenue and then we slice up the pie differently.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Some of it may be spent now because, like he mentioned a whole lot of infrastructure funds, but he omitted mentioning the other funds which I talked about in my reply earlier – like, for example, the Pioneer Generation Fund, the Merdeka Generation Fund and the GST Voucher Fund, which we draw down and we draw down now for today's generation; and some of it may be later.

sections.label: Goh Keng Swee austerity measures
sections.summary: In 1959 Dr Goh Keng Swee became Minister for Finance and implemented austerity measures including pay cuts for civil servants and Ministers.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In 1959, when the PAP Government first took office, Dr Goh Keng Swee was appointed Minister for Finance and he immediately discovered that the Treasury was bare and he had to implement immediate austerity measures, including pay cuts for civil servants and Ministers.

sections.label: Elected presidency created
sections.summary: In January 1991, after the election, the Constitution was amended to create the elected presidency.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: After the election, in January 1991, we amended the Constitution to create the elected presidency.

sections.label: Fifth Schedule entities listed
sections.summary: The Fifth Schedule entities are MAS, Temasek, GIC, CPF, JTC and HDB.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Fifth Schedule because it is a Fifth Schedule attached at the back of the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: These Fifth Schedule entities are MAS, Temasek, GIC, CPF, JTC, HDB.

sections.label: 50-50 reserves split
sections.summary: A split of 50-50 was arrived at for providing for the future while enabling the present generation to benefit from the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, the question is, how much to provide for the future while also enabling the present generation to benefit from the Reserves?

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: There is no magic rule to this, but we arrived at a split of 50-50.

sections.label: Including capital gains
sections.summary: It was decided to consider not just interest and dividends but also to include capital gains.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, in that circumstance, can we say, returns from the investment is zero?

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, we decided we should consider not just the interest and dividends but also include capital gains as well.

sections.label: NIR spending and NIRC
