sections.summary: In 2008 the Constitution was amended to specify spending out of NIR instead of NII, keeping the 50% rule, and this amount was called the NIRC.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, we studied them, we modelled our rules on these ideas, taking into account our political and constitutional context, which makes it much more complicated for us to implement than, say, a US university.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, in 2008, we amended the Constitution again to specify that the Government would spend out of NIR, instead of NII.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But we kept the 50% rule, so the Government could spend 50% of NIR instead of 50% of NII.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And we called this amount which a government can draw from the Reserves and add to the annual Budget to spend, the NIRC.

sections.label: COVID-19 Past Reserves drawdown
sections.summary: Singapore sought approval to draw up to $69 billion from Past Reserves for COVID-19, and drew about $40 billion.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The next crisis, COVID-19, when it hit us, that was on a different scale altogether.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We sought the President's approval successively to draw up to $69 billion from our Past Reserves for medical facilities, testing, vaccines, support schemes and Assurance Packages.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In the end, we actually drew down about $40 billion.

sections.label: Constitutional 50/50 spending rule
sections.summary: The spending rule settled on and enshrined in the Constitution is 50/50.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: The spending rule which we have settled on and enshrined in the Constitution is 50/50.

sections.label: Assumed long-term real return
sections.summary: The passage assumes a long-term expected real return of 4%.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Let us assume a long-term expected real return of 4%.

sections.label: Reserves grow at 2%
sections.summary: Under the 50/50 rule, 2% goes back into the Reserves, which grow at 2% per year.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, just because the balance is sitting there does not mean you can take it home.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: So, 50/50, 2% goes back into the Reserves, the Reserves will grow, all things going well, at 2% per year.

sections.label: NIRC contribution to Budget
sections.summary: The NIRC contribution to the Budget will be about the same every year, about 3.5% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: It is not getting bigger and bigger, more and more Reserves, while the GDP languishes.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And so, the contribution to our Budget, NIRC, will be about the same every year, about 3.5% of GDP.

sections.label: Spending within means, GST
sections.summary: Each generation must spend within its means, requiring tax revisions such as the GST raised to 9%.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: But each generation must spend within our means, and each generation has been able to spend within our means and, even this generation, we can spend within our means.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: It does mean that, from time to time, we have to revise our taxes, raise some of them, like the GST, which we have just raised to 9%, and we have powerful reasons for doing so, which have been extensively debated.

sections.label: Budget draw from Past Reserves
sections.summary: The Budget included the Job Support Scheme and a plan to draw $4.9 billion from the Past Reserves.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In the Budget – this is a Budget where we had the Job Support Scheme – and we were going to draw $4.9 billion from the Past Reserves.

sections.label: Returning money to Past Reserves
sections.summary: The Government prudently returned $4 billion to Past Reserves that it had taken in 2009, with shared commitment to safeguard them.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: It has prudently put back into Past Reserves the $4 billion that the Government took in 2009." So, this is how a responsible Opposition conducts itself.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: There was a common commitment to safeguard our Past Reserves and a recognition, a shared recognition, that they are a strategic asset only to be used for unprecedented circumstances.

sections.label: Lee Kuan Yew and two key scheme
sections.summary: Lee Kuan Yew knew money would never be enough and raising taxes politically tough, so he designed the two key scheme.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: We all want more things to be done, but we also know – and Mr Lee Kuan Yew knew – that that money would always be not enough.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: And he knew that it would always be politically tough to raise taxes and that is why he and his colleagues designed and implemented the "two key" scheme.

sections.label: 2001 NII 50% rule debate
sections.summary: In 2001 the 50% rule on NII was instituted and the Constitution amended, with Lee Kuan Yew intervening in the debate.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: In 2001, when we instituted the 50% rule applied to the NII and amended the Constitution, Mr Lee Kuan Yew intervened in the debate because some MPs were proposing good causes to spend the money on, particularly old people.

sections.label: Ballot box on Reserves
sections.summary: Other parties wanting to dip into Reserves more should bring it to the ballot box and state it upfront.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: If any other political party thinks that this is not the right approach, if they truly believe that we should dip into our Reserves more, then bring it to the ballot box, put it upfront, say you want to touch, you want to spend, you want to shift the rules.

sections.label: IPS survey on trust in PAP
sections.summary: The IPS survey showed high confidence in the PAP Government's management of the Reserves, a vital responsibility.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Because and if I may come back to the IPS survey which we referred to and which you still have in your hands, it was not just a survey of the trust for input on Reserves but trust in the PAP Government in general.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: If you look at the paragraph under paragraph 3.3, it says, "In the case of the PAP Government, the statement was modified to refer to the level of trust in it to manage the Reserves." In other words, Singaporeans have high confidence in the PAP Government's management of the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: Taking a long-term view of the Reserves, striking the right balance between present and future needs, these are vital responsibilities of any Singapore government.

sentences.speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
sentences.text: I have spent 40 years of my life stewarding, safeguarding, improving the system and continuing the work of those who had come before me.

sections.label: PAP Government not returning $40 billion
sections.summary: The speaker recalls telling Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong that different times call for different measures, and says the PAP Government is not returning the $40 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: My response to Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong at that time, if I recall, was different times call for different measures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: And a good example manifesting that point is the fact that the PAP Government is not returning the $40 billion back.

sections.label: NIRC system sustainability and expected returns
sections.summary: The speaker returns to Finance Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam's 2015 speech that the modified NIRC system was made sustainable with no bias toward over-optimism in expected returns.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: The first really takes off from the exchange I had with the hon Member Mr Neil Parekh about a concern the Prime Minister raised about how the returns can be volatile.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I return to the speech made by Finance Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam in 2015, and I quote, "The NIRC system, after it was modified in 2008, we paid particular attention to ensuring the system will be sustainable and that there is no bias in favour of over-optimism in expected returns and thus, the likelihood of facing a situation where actual returns are, in fact, much lower than expected returns." I am not trying to be obtuse about the point, but I think it is important to understand the NIRC framework.

sections.label: Prime Minister clarifying NIRC conservatism
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Prime Minister to clarify whether the position may not be as conservative as Finance Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam suggested in 2015, which would affect views on NIRC use.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: But what the Prime Minister is suggesting is that it may not be as conservative as Finance Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam suggested in 2015.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: So, if the Prime Minister could clarify what is the position, because it will cause to turn anybody's view on how the NIRC ought to be used.

sections.label: Repeated land sales and conversion position
sections.summary: The speaker disagreed with the Leader of the House on the WP position and asks the Prime Minister how repeated land sales cohere with his position that land is just a conversion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I made it clear to the Leader of the House that I disagreed with how she had put the WP position.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: But again, it will be helpful if the Prime Minister can share with this House if a single piece of land is sold repeatedly for as long as the lease lasts – how does that cohere with the Prime Minister's position that land is just a conversion?

sections.label: GST rate increases and WP opposition
sections.summary: The speaker says he introduced GST at 3% and pushed it to 5%, Tharman Shanmugaratnam took it to 7%, and ex-MP Leon Perera said the WP opposes going to 9%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: Introducing it at 3%, pushing it up from 3% to 5%, which I did, going from 5% to 7%, which Tharman Shanmugaratnam did as Finance Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: And we reminded the WP of this, only to be told by their ex-MP, Mr Leon Perera, that now that it has reached 7%, they do not oppose that, but they oppose it going to 9%.

sections.label: Land sale proceeds as stream of payments
sections.summary: The speaker says every time he sells land he puts money into the Reserves, but not all today, as a stream of payments 30 years apart.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: Yes, of course, every time I sell the land, I put money into the Reserves, but I am not putting the money into the Reserves all today.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
sentences.text: I am putting it in a stream of payments, 30 years apart.

sections.label: PAP policies and Reserve accumulation
sections.summary: The speaker says PAP policies are not that bad but proposes slowing Reserve accumulation to postpone tax increases and help Singaporeans cope with inflation and rising property prices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The PAP policies are not that bad, but we think we can do better together.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: This is because what we are proposing is only going to slow down the Reserve accumulation and in exchange for that, to postpone the taxes increases so as to help Singaporeans cope with inflation and rising property prices.

sections.label: Government not disclosing Reserves figure
sections.summary: The speaker says many Singaporeans will remain disappointed that the Government probably still will not disclose the figure of the financial Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: After today's debate, I am sure that many Singaporeans will continue to be disappointed, that this Government probably would still not want to disclose the figure of our financial Reserves.

sections.label: MAS OFR to GDP
sections.summary: MAS has OFR equivalent to 80% of Singapore's GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: MAS has OFR equivalent to 80% of our GDP.

sections.label: Confidence and knowledge of Reserves
sections.summary: The speaker hopes Singaporeans do not need to wait another 56 man years for an answer about the financial Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Full confidence and full knowledge of what our country has in the Reserves.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: I hope Singaporeans do not need to wait for another 56 man years before they get an answer about our financial Reserves at least.

sections.label: Financial reserves amount
sections.summary: The speaker states that Singapore's financial reserves amount to more than $1.2 trillion at least.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: First, our financial reserves amount to more than $1.2 trillion at least.

sections.label: Cost of Reserve accumulation
sections.summary: The second takeaway is that the continued accumulation of Reserves comes at a cost to Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The second takeaway is that the continued accumulation of Reserves comes at a cost to Singaporeans.

sections.label: Slowing Reserve accumulation marginally
sections.summary: The passage states that Reserves need not be drawn down, only the rate of Reserve accumulation slowed marginally for better economic outcomes for Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The third takeaway is, fortunately, we actually do not need to draw down our Reserves, but just slow down the rate of Reserve accumulation marginally to produce much better economic outcomes for Singaporeans.

sections.label: Government financial statements amounts
sections.summary: The passage states that, according to checking of Government financial statements, the amount is probably about $50 billion a year, $50 billion to $100 billion depending on the year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: According to my checking of the Government financial statements and all that, probably about $50 billion a year, $50 billion to $100 billion, depending on which year it is.

sections.label: Household expenditures survey bottom households
sections.summary: The passage states the 2020 household expenditures survey shows bottom 20% and second quintile household expenses and income, suggesting the bottom 40% struggle while Government accumulated savings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The household expenditures survey in 2020 shows that the bottom 20% of Singapore households by income, in 2018, spent $2,235 in expenses and got $2,570 in income, including employer CPF.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: This means that after deducting the employer and employee CPF contributions, the bottom 20% of households, or more than 200,000 households are essentially, in deficit and must rely on Government handouts, charity or loans from legal or illegal moneylenders to survive.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: For the second quintile, it is $3,752 in expenses versus $5,981 in income, again, including employer CPF.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: The survey suggests that the bottom 40% of Singapore households are really struggling to survive while the Government has accumulated lots of savings or reserves.

sections.label: Disclose Reserves and utilise resources
sections.summary: The passage proposes disclosing the total amount of Reserves and actively utilising the country's substantial financial resources to reduce the people's financial burden and improve quality of life.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: First, disclose the total amount of our Reserves, allowing the people to have an accurate understanding of our finances and related policies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Second, actively utilise our country's substantial financial resources to help reduce the financial burden on the people and improve their quality of life.

sections.label: PSP estimate of total Reserves
sections.summary: The passage states that, according to PSP's estimation, excluding land reserves, total Reserves reached $1.2 trillion, earning nearly $50 billion in net investment returns yearly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: According to PSP's estimation, excluding land reserves, our total Reserves has reached $1.2 trillion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Furthermore, from these assets, we earn nearly $50 billion in net investment returns each year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: We have four amendments proposed by Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

sentences.text: Amendment No 1 is, "In line 1, to delete 'review' and insert 'ensure'."
